source.title: Scaling Laws for Associative Memories
source.authors: Vivien Cabannes; Elvis Dohmatob; A. Bietti

record.tranche_reason: Tests capacity limits and interference in a toy associative-memory model with random embeddings, using Zipf-distributed input frequencies and error scaling rather than the original Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports results about optimization choices, embedding learning, and training dynamics. Rows below retain results that bear on memory capacity, interference, or the geometry of stored associations; cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: This paper does not test superposition as the versions state it. It analyses capacity scaling laws for a linear outer-product associative memory W=Σq(x)u e^T. Superposition is imposed by construction: N fixed random embeddings packed into d<N dimensions. It never asks whether a trained network chooses to superpose sparse features, never varies feature sparsity, and never measures learned feature geometry. Its measure is generalization error versus d and T for designed or optimizer-induced storage schemes. That is a related construct (memory capacity under interference), so its findings go under fits_no_version. Elhage et al. (2022) is cited once, in an appendix remark on compensation mechanisms.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors derive scaling laws in data size T and capacity d for outer-product associative memories as a proxy for transformer inner layers. They argue uniformly weighted outer products work best and that small batches with large learning rates help. Under hardware and stability constraints they find Adam and layer norm useful. The claim that learned embeddings greatly increase capacity comes from Section 4.2, not the conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: Uses outer-product associative memories, random or learned token embeddings, Zipf-distributed inputs, and generalization error/scaling analyses; it does not reproduce the original Toy Models of Superposition intervention or feature-geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with dimension d, sample size T, Zipf exponent α, weighting exponent ρ, threshold P, and whether embeddings are random or learned. The paper also reports training-storage behavior varying with learning rate and batch size.

fits_no_version.finding: A d×d outer-product memory with random embeddings stores about d (≈d/log d) associations. Error from interference follows d^{-(α-1)} at best for Zipf inputs. Uniform storage shows an overflow regime when d is well below N.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear associative memories with random quasi-orthogonal embeddings have capacity linear in d, with interference-driven recall error scaling as d^{-(α-1)} under Zipf data.

fits_no_version.finding: When embeddings are learned, optimization merges inputs sharing an output into one direction. This gives zero error at d=2 for N=100, M=5 (Figure 8), versus d≥N needed with random embeddings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned embeddings raise associative-memory capacity by collapsing inputs onto output-class directions rather than superposing them.

record.problems: The evidence is from a simplified synthetic associative-memory model, not an LLM. It does not directly measure co-activation sparsity or the geometry of feature directions. Several plotted results are described qualitatively rather than reported as individual numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: Other optimization comparisons and additional training-dynamics figures (Figures 4–7 and 10–16) are not separately cataloged because they focus on optimizer behavior or memory-learning dynamics rather than directly measuring the tested feature-capacity or geometry claim.

untested.parts: Whether trained networks adopt superposition, any sparsity dependence, feature importance or geometry of learned feature directions. Superposition is imposed, not observed.
All; no neurons or polysemanticity are examined.
All; no LLM activations or SAEs.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 and V1 'supports' labels are dropped. The model's 'superposition' is by construction, from random embeddings in d<N, so the results cannot show whether superposition arises or how it is geometrically organized. Lemma 1, an exponential number of quasi-orthogonal vectors in R^d, is a background existence result, not a test. ICLR 2024.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly measure feature co-activation sparsity, angles between learned feature directions, or a geometric transition to regular superposition configurations. Its Zipf-distributed token frequencies and associative mappings are not a direct test of the original feature-superposition setup.
Does not measure neuron polysemanticity or whether particular neurons are dedicated to important features.
Does not study polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Does not analyze LLM activations, feature spread across neurons, or SAE-recoverable features.
Does not evaluate whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical.
Does not test whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: associative memory model (2)
rows.size_stated: dimension d; no single size stated
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical characterization of generalization error with random input embeddings and random spherical output embeddings.

conditions.value: independent ex ~ N(0,I); unembeddings uniform on the sphere

rows.value: Theorem 1 gives an upper bound involving the probability mass of inputs with dq(x)^2 below a threshold set by Q∞ and a lower bound involving inputs with 3(d+1)q(x)^2 ≤ Q∞; the paper interprets Q∞ as the strongest competing-class interference.
rows.note: An analytic result for this model: interference from superposed outer-product memories can cause recall errors, with error depending on dimension and memory weights.
rows.check: Analytic error bound for a memory with superposition imposed by random embeddings. It measures recall error, not whether features are stored superposed or how. It does not bear on V1's sparsity transition or geometry.

rows.subject: associative memory model (2)
rows.operation_detail: Derived error scaling for frequency-weighted memories q(x)=p(x)^ρ without thresholding.
rows.measure: Expected generalization error as dimension d varies
rows.value: For 2ρα > 1, the error scales, up to poly-logarithmic factors and constants, as d^{-(α−1)/(2ρα)}; for 2ρα = 1 or 2ρα < 1 the paper gives separate N-dependent regimes.
rows.note: Shows that frequency weighting changes the capacity/error scaling; the stated power of d applies in the 2ρα > 1 regime.
rows.check: Derived scaling law for a hand-designed weighting scheme q=p^ρ. It is a property of the scheme chosen by the authors, not an emergent superposition measurement.

rows.subject: associative memory model (2)
rows.operation_detail: Derived error scaling for thresholded, frequency-weighted memories q(x)=p(x)^ρ 1x∈[P].
rows.measure: Expected generalization error as dimension d varies
rows.value: The error scales as d^{-(α−1)/(2ρα+1)}, up to logarithmic factors; for ρ=0 and P ≃ d, it scales as d^{−α+1}, which the paper calls optimal.
rows.note: The thresholded scheme stores a selected set of associations and yields a different capacity scaling from unthresholded frequency weighting.
rows.check: Derived scaling for a hand-designed thresholded scheme. Storing only the top-P items is the authors' choice, not an observed allocation by a trained network.

rows.subject: associative memory model (2)
rows.operation_detail: Derived behavior for uniform unthresholded storage q(x)=1.
rows.value: The paper states that the error is high when d < N and falls rapidly toward zero when d > N; Proposition 2 describes the ρ=0 limit as going to zero if and only if d is bigger than N.
rows.note: The sharp capacity behavior is for this finite-N setting and uniform storage, not a direct measurement of feature-direction geometry.
rows.check: Theoretical d-versus-N capacity transition for uniform storage. The transition is in dimension relative to item count, not in feature sparsity as V1 describes.

rows.subject: associative memory model (2)
rows.operation_detail: Numerical generalization-error comparison of uniform storage, frequency weighting, and thresholded storage.
rows.value: The caption reports q0 as a zero-one-type curve with high error below N and rapid decrease above N; q1 decreases as d^{−1/4}; q0,P decreases as d^{−1} until d/8>N.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 3 reports averages over 100 runs; no uncertainty value stated for this panel.
rows.note: The figure caption states the trends and the predicted powers; individual plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Numerical check of the designed schemes (Figure 3 right). It compares the authors' storage schemes with each other; no superposition geometry is measured.

rows.subject: associative memory model (2)
rows.size_stated: N=100, M=5; d and T varied
rows.operation_detail: Numerical generalization-error comparison for uniform storage q0 and frequency-weighted storage q1.
rows.measure: Generalization error versus d and T
rows.value: The caption says q0 has large error from memory overflow when d is small; q1 avoids overflow and has lower error for small d and large T, but at large d it allocates too little memory to rare associations and has higher error than q0.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 3 reports averages over 100 runs; no uncertainty value stated for these panels.
rows.note: The outcome depends on dimension and the frequency-weighting scheme.
rows.check: Comparison of two designed schemes (Figure 3 left/middle). It was marked 'partial', but there is no version effect to grade; the dependence on d is a scheme comparison.

rows.subject: associative memory model (2)
rows.operation_detail: Empirical scaling experiment for the thresholded scheme q=1x≤d/8.
rows.measure: Generalization error versus d and T
rows.value: Figure 1 reports empirical validation of E(fq) ≍ d^{−α+1}+T^{−1+1/α}; with α=2 this is d^{−1}+T^{−1/2}.
rows.uncertainty: Experiments averaged over 100 runs; standard deviations are shown.
rows.note: This is an empirical check of the scaling law for the chosen thresholded associative-memory scheme.
rows.check: Empirical validation of the scaling law for one designed thresholded scheme (Figure 1). This is the study's own theory being checked against itself.

rows.subject: associative memory model (2)
rows.operation_detail: Learned input embeddings with optimization; the paper reports a solution with zero generalization error.
rows.baseline: Random embeddings required d ≥ N for zero generalization error in the stated comparison.
rows.note: The paper says learned input embeddings can be set to the output embedding for the associated class; this changes the storage setup rather than demonstrating overlapping feature directions.
rows.check: With learned embeddings, inputs collapse onto the output embedding of their class (ex=u_f*(x), Figure 8). The model stores 5 class directions in d=2, not 100 superposed features. This is not evidence on V1, and the row's 'partial' state has no version effect to grade.

relation.reason: The paper describes superposed memories and discusses interference compensation in Appendix A.9.1, referring to Elhage et al. (2022), without testing the catalog's claim versions.

tranche.reason: Associative-memory error and capacity scaling do not test any listed claim version. Mixing associations in a matrix is imposed by the model; the learned-embedding result merges inputs sharing an output.

source_check.notes: Figure 8 learns input embeddings and output unembeddings. Its zero-error result concerns classification after merging same-output inputs, rather than recovery of 100 distinct superposed features.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Random embeddings and the tested associative-memory schemes
reader_labels.reason: Finite capacity produces interference-related recall error, and the error scaling changes with dimension and memory weighting (R1–R7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The model achieves zero error at d=2 in the reported N=100 task, showing that the random-embedding capacity behavior does not hold unchanged when embeddings are learned (R8).
